newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish premier battles floods, heavy criticism.
newsitem.headline: Polish premier battles floods, heavy criticism.

text.p: Poland's prime minister defended his government's response to disastrous floods on Wednesday under fierce opposition attack in parliament.
Introducing 22 laws to rush funds and aid to hundreds of suffering communities, Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said the worst was slowly ending and Polish society had withstood the test.
"This flood, which cannot be compared with anything in the past, has not thrown us on our knees," he told an emergency session of the lower house.

Deputies began the gathering with a moment's silence for at least 39 people who have died and hundreds of thousands whose homes and livelihoods have been wrecked. The catastrophe, which began with huge downpours early last week, is still not over.

Cimoszewicz said the damage was incalculable, but water had swamped 4,500 sq km (1,700 square miles), of which more than two-fifths were still inundated. It had struck 40,000 farms, 86 towns and 875 villages.
He proposed bills including a change in the current budget to allow more borrowing at home and abroad, rapid cash payments to affected households, and reserve grain supplies to farmers.

Defending official responses to what he said had been an unexpectedly huge calamity, the ex-communist Cimoszewicz told deputies not to make political capital out of the crisis, to focus on current priorities and leave judgements for later.
But the opposition would not let him off the hook before September 21 elections in which his Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) is challenged by a bloc led by the Solidarity trade union.
Centrist opposition leader Bronislaw Geremek said the government had failed the people in their hour of need.

"As a result of government inaction, the authority of the state was eroded and weakened. Citizens' confidence in the state vanished," Geremek said, especially reproaching the government for failing to declare a state of emergency.
He said that if the cabinet had adopted emergency powers, it may have overcome the resistance of panicked local villagers and blown up dykes on the Odra River upstream from Wroclaw.

This would have flooded villages but may have saved the historic city of 650,000 people, still partially flooded on Wednesday, and other communities still being struck by a slowly-lessening wave surging north on the Odra, he said. @

Cimoszewicz reassured Poles there had been no signs of contagious disease, only food poisoning, in areas where water was retreating to reveal smashed homes, broken bridges and chewed-up roads strewn with sewage and dead animals.

As the government faced a massive task of urgent relief and longer-term reconstruction, it trod a tightrope between the need for resources and the danger of harming economic stability -- underlined by the zloty's five percent fall on Tuesday.
On Wednesday the currency partially steadied.
The government proposed amending this year's budget to get an additional 2.5 billion zloty ($710 million) borrowing limit in the central bank to ensure it had enough ready money.
It was also seeking an increase in its foreign borrowing limits to allow a $300 million World Bank loan.

Largely by yanking money from other budget goals and halting capital projects, the government has already lined up 650 million zlotys for flood relief and was determined to rebuild as much as possible in the months before winter.
It was not clear if voting on the bills would be over on Thursday or drag on into the weekend as fierce controversy continued.
Cimoszewicz thanked other countries rallying to Poland's aid, notably neighbouring Germany and the European Union, to which he had addressed a list of needs.
Poland was on Wednesday formally invited to begin EU entry talks, a triumph following hard on its inclusion in the first three former Soviet bloc states bound for NATO.
At any other time, Poland would have been basking in its success. The floods robbed the moment of its savour.
($ = 3.516 Polish Zlotys)
